claim: Heat stress triggers extensive endocytic downregulation of various plasma membrane cargo proteins in yeast.
source: Previously, we found that certain environmental changes elicit highly-specific surface remodeling programs, such as the methionine-induced endocytic down-regulation of the methionine transporter Mup1 (Lin et al., 2008). In contrast, other environmental changes can stimulate global surface remodeling programs, such as the TORC1-mediated tuning of PM protein composition by activation of the ART adaptor network (MacGurn et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing cargo trafficking and degradation at different temperatures, as described in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Most plasma membrane cargoes undergo endocytosis followed by vacuolar trafficking during heat stress at 38°C for 60 min.
source: In general, most cargoes were observed to undergo endocytosis followed by vacuolar trafficking (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2) and degradation (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5), although a few cargoes appeared to be stable (Pdr5, Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 5) or induced during heat stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by microscopy data in Figure 1A and degradation data in Figure 1B showing cargo trafficking to the vacuole.

claim: Heat-induced endocytic downregulation occurs with varying kinetics and efficiency for diverse cargoes including amino acid transporters (Mup1, Lyp1, Dip5), hexose transporters (Hxt3), G-protein coupled receptors (Ste3) and proton pumps (Pma1).
source: This heat-induced endocytic downregulation was observed with varying kinetics and efficiency for many diverse cargoes including amino acid transporters (Mup1, Lyp1, Dip5), hexose transporters (Hxt3), G-protein coupled receptors (Ste3) and proton pumps (Pma1) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing degradation kinetics for multiple cargo types in Figure 1B.

claim: Pdr5 is stable during heat stress.
source: In general, most cargoes were observed to undergo endocytosis followed by vacuolar trafficking (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2) and degradation (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5), although a few cargoes appeared to be stable (Pdr5, Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 5) or induced during heat stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1B showing Pdr5 protein levels remain constant during heat stress.

claim: Ethanol stress triggers endocytic downregulation of Can1 and Mup1 but has little effect on Lyp1 stability.
source: For example, ethanol stress triggered the endocytic downregulation of the arginine transporter Can1 and the methionine transporter Mup1, but had little effect on the surface stability of Lyp1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7 showing differential cargo responses to ethanol stress.

claim: Oxidative stress triggers endocytic downregulation of Lyp1 and Can1 but has little effect on Mup1 stability.
source: In contrast, oxidative stress triggered the endocytic downregulation of Lyp1 and Can1 but had little effect on the surface stability of Mup1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7 showing differential cargo responses to oxidative stress.

claim: Different cargoes exhibit different thermostability profiles.
source: We found that different cargoes exhibited a range of thermostabilities (Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 8) suggesting heat stress triggers thermo-instability that is cargo-intrinsic.
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis data showing different half-lives for different cargoes at various temperatures, presented in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: Glycerol enhances the thermostability of Lyp1.
source: Importantly, glycerol enhanced the thermostability of Lyp1 (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 9) but did not stabilize the methionine-induced endocytic downregulation of the methionine transporter Mup1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1C showing reduced Lyp1 degradation in the presence of glycerol during heat stress.

claim: Glycerol does not stabilize methionine-induced endocytic downregulation of Mup1.
source: Importantly, glycerol enhanced the thermostability of Lyp1 (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 9) but did not stabilize the methionine-induced endocytic downregulation of the methionine transporter Mup1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 10 showing Mup1 degradation occurs similarly with or without glycerol in the presence of methionine.

claim: Glycerol is known to promote/stabilize protein folding and function as a chemical chaperone.
source: To test this idea, we performed thermostability analysis of the highly thermo-labile lysine transporter Lyp1 in the presence of glycerol, which is known to promote/stabilize protein folding and function as a chemical chaperone (Bernier et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bernier et al., 2004.

claim: Lyp1 detergent solubility is significantly reduced during heat stress.
source: While Pdr5 did not exhibit a significant change in detergent solubility at high temperature (Figure 1D, left), Lyp1 detergent solubility was significantly reduced during heat stress (Figure 1D, right) indicating that Lyp1, but not Pdr5, may be misfolding or aggregating at high temperature.
evidence: The claim is supported by detergent solubility assay data in Figure 1D showing reduced Lyp1 in the soluble fraction at 40°C.

claim: Pdr5 does not exhibit a significant change in detergent solubility at high temperature.
source: While Pdr5 did not exhibit a significant change in detergent solubility at high temperature (Figure 1D, left), Lyp1 detergent solubility was significantly reduced during heat stress (Figure 1D, right) indicating that Lyp1, but not Pdr5, may be misfolding or aggregating at high temperature.
evidence: The claim is supported by detergent solubility assay data in Figure 1D showing similar Pdr5 solubility at 26°C and 40°C.

claim: Detergent-insoluble Lyp1 migrates to the bottom of a sucrose gradient, suggesting Lyp1 aggregation during heat stress.
source: Importantly, while detergent-soluble cargo in the S40 floated on the sucrose gradient, detergent-insoluble Lyp1 in the P40 fraction migrated to the bottom of the sucrose gradient (Figure 1E), suggesting Lyp1 aggregation during heat stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by sucrose gradient fractionation data in Figure 1E showing Lyp1 in the bottom fraction of the gradient.

claim: Mutations in either WW2 or WW3 domains of Rsp5 significantly abrogate the heat-induced endocytic response.
source: While the WW1 domain of Rsp5 was dispensable for heat-induced cargo degradation, mutations in either WW2 or WW3 significantly abrogated the endocytic response (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and Western blot data in Figure 2A-C showing cargo accumulation at the plasma membrane in rsp5-ww2 and rsp5-ww3 mutants during heat stress.

claim: The WW1 domain of Rsp5 is dispensable for heat-induced cargo degradation.
source: While the WW1 domain of Rsp5 was dispensable for heat-induced cargo degradation, mutations in either WW2 or WW3 significantly abrogated the endocytic response (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 2 showing that rsp5-ww1 mutants do not exhibit defects in cargo degradation during heat stress.

claim: rsp5-ww2 and rsp5-ww3 mutants are extremely temperature sensitive and fail to grow at 38°C.
source: While rsp5-ww1 mutants did not exhibit any observable temperature sensitivity defect, rsp5-ww2 and rsp5-ww3 mutants were extremely temperature sensitive and failed to grow at 38°C (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data in Figure 2D showing no growth of rsp5-ww2 and rsp5-ww3 mutants at 38°C.

claim: rsp5-ww1 mutants do not exhibit any observable temperature sensitivity defect.
source: While rsp5-ww1 mutants did not exhibit any observable temperature sensitivity defect, rsp5-ww2 and rsp5-ww3 mutants were extremely temperature sensitive and failed to grow at 38°C (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data in Figure 2D showing normal growth of rsp5-ww1 mutants at 38°C.

claim: rsp5-ww2 and rsp5-ww3 mutant cells exhibit a significant fraction of the population that stains PI-positive in response to heat stress.
source: After three hours at 40°C, wildtype and rsp5-ww1 yeast cells did not exhibit any significant PI staining (Figure 3B,C). In contrast, rsp5-ww2 and rsp5-ww3 mutant cells exhibited a significant fraction of the population that stained PI-positive in response to heat stress (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B,C showing increased PI staining in rsp5-ww2 and rsp5-ww3 mutants after heat stress.

claim: Wildtype and rsp5-ww1 yeast cells do not exhibit any significant PI staining after three hours at 40°C.
source: After three hours at 40°C, wildtype and rsp5-ww1 yeast cells did not exhibit any significant PI staining (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B,C showing minimal PI staining in wildtype and rsp5-ww1 cells after heat stress.

claim: Mutations that abrogate endocytosis (Δend3, Δrvs167) result in significant PI staining in response to heat stress.
source: While mutations that abrogate endocytosis (Δend3, Δrvs167) resulted in significant PI staining in response to heat stress, mutant cells defective for downstream trafficking events such as endosomal sorting and multivesicular body biogenesis (Δvps23), endosomal-vacuolar fusion (Δvam3), and vacuolar degradation (Δpep4) exhibited negligible PI staining in response to heat stress (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3C showing increased PI staining in Δend3 and Δrvs167 mutants after heat stress.

claim: Mutant cells defective for endosomal sorting and multivesicular body biogenesis (Δvps23), endosomal-vacuolar fusion (Δvam3), and vacuolar degradation (Δpep4) exhibit negligible PI staining in response to heat stress.
source: While mutations that abrogate endocytosis (Δend3, Δrvs167) resulted in significant PI staining in response to heat stress, mutant cells defective for downstream trafficking events such as endosomal sorting and multivesicular body biogenesis (Δvps23), endosomal-vacuolar fusion (Δvam3), and vacuolar degradation (Δpep4) exhibited negligible PI staining in response to heat stress (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3C showing minimal PI staining in Δvps23, Δvam3, and Δpep4 mutants after heat stress.

claim: Plasma membrane clearance is the critical event protecting cells from heat-induced loss of PM integrity.
source: These results indicate that plasma membrane clearance is the critical event protecting cells from heat-induced loss of PM integrity, while downstream sorting and trafficking events are dispensable.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that endocytosis mutants show PI staining while downstream trafficking mutants do not.

claim: Δart1 yeast cells are temperature sensitive for growth at 38°C.
source: While most ART (arrestin-related trafficking adaptor) family proteins were found to be dispensable for growth at high temperatures, Δart1 yeast cells were temperature sensitive for growth at 38°C similar to rsp5-ww2 and rsp5-ww3 mutant cells (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data in Figure 4A showing reduced growth of Δart1 cells at 38°C.

claim: Heat-induced endocytosis and vacuolar degradation of most cargoes is Art1-independent, with the exception of Lyp1.
source: Importantly, our analysis revealed that heat-induced endocytosis and vacuolar degradation of most cargoes is Art1-independent, with the exception of the lysine transporter Lyp1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data in Figure 4B showing that Can1 and Mup1 traffic to the vacuole in Δart1 cells during heat stress, but Lyp1 does not.

claim: Lyp1 endocytosis and vacuolar degradation is abrogated in the absence of Art1.
source: In contrast to other cargoes, Lyp1 endocytosis and vacuolar degradation is abrogated in the absence of Art1 (Figure 4B,C), underscoring the cargo-specific role Art1 plays in the heat-induced endocytic response.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and Western blot data in Figure 4B,C showing Lyp1 accumulation at the plasma membrane in Δart1 cells during heat stress.

claim: Art1-GFP translocates to the plasma membrane in response to heat stress.
source: Consistent with its role in the heat-induced endocytic response, we found that Art1-GFP translocates to the PM in response to heat stress (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing Art1-GFP localization at the plasma membrane after heat stress.

claim: Deletion of ART2 in Δart1 mutant cells results in an enhanced temperature sensitivity phenotype.
source: Although Δart2 mutant cells did not exhibit any temperature sensitive phenotypes, we found that deletion of ART2 in Δart1 mutant cells resulted in an enhanced temperature sensitivity phenotype (Figure 4D) that correlated with increased Lyp1 accumulation in the Δart1Δart2 double mutant (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data in Figure 4D showing reduced growth of Δart1Δart2 double mutants compared to Δart1 single mutants at elevated temperatures.

claim: Δart1Δart2 double mutants show increased Lyp1 accumulation compared to Δart1 single mutants.
source: Although Δart2 mutant cells did not exhibit any temperature sensitive phenotypes, we found that deletion of ART2 in Δart1 mutant cells resulted in an enhanced temperature sensitivity phenotype (Figure 4D) that correlated with increased Lyp1 accumulation in the Δart1Δart2 double mutant (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4C showing higher Lyp1 levels in Δart1Δart2 cells compared to Δart1 cells during heat stress.

claim: Δart1 mutant cells exhibit a slight loss of PM integrity (∼18% of the cells are PI-positive following 40°C for 3 hr).
source: Although Δart1 mutant cells exhibited a slight loss of PM integrity (∼18% of the cells are PI-positive following 40°C for 3 hr), the other adaptor mutants tested exhibited no defects in PM integrity in response to heat stress (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4E showing approximately 18% PI-positive cells in Δart1 mutants after heat stress.

claim: Striking synthetic defects in PM integrity are observed when Δart1 is combined with deletion of other ART genes.
source: However, striking synthetic defects were observed when Δart1 was combined with deletion of other ART genes (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4E,F showing increased PI staining in multiple ART deletion mutants compared to single mutants.

claim: Loss of multiple ART genes effectively blocks Mup1 turnover in response to heat stress.
source: Furthermore, while ART1 and ART2 are dispensable for Mup1 trafficking to the vacuole in response to heat stress (Figure 4B and data not shown), the loss of multiple ART genes effectively blocks Mup1 turnover in response to heat stress (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data in Figure 4G showing Mup1 accumulation at the plasma membrane in Δart1Δart2Δart3Δart4Δart5Δart6Δart9 cells during heat stress.

claim: Loss of Lyp1 partially suppresses the temperature sensitive phenotype of Δart1 mutant cells.
source: To do this, we analyzed temperature sensitivity of Δart1Δlyp1 mutant cells and, to our surprise, found that loss of Lyp1 partially suppressed the temperature sensitive phenotype of Δart1 mutant cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data in Figure 5A showing improved growth of Δart1Δlyp1 double mutants compared to Δart1 single mutants at elevated temperatures.

claim: Lyp1 accumulation at the plasma membrane during heat stress is toxic.
source: This result suggests that Lyp1 accumulation at the PM during heat stress is toxic and significantly contributes to the temperature sensitive phenotype of Δart1 mutant cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that deletion of Lyp1 suppresses the temperature sensitivity of Δart1 mutants.

claim: Lyp1 expression correlates with temperature sensitivity in Δart1Δlyp1 cells expressing Lyp1 from different promoters.
source: Importantly, we found that Lyp1 expression correlated with temperature sensitivity in Δart1Δlyp1 cells, where the expressed Lyp1 could not be efficiently internalized in response to heat stress (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay and Western blot data in Figure 5B showing that higher Lyp1 expression levels correlate with increased temperature sensitivity.

claim: High expression levels of Lyp1-K10XR result in increased temperature sensitivity even in wildtype cells.
source: High expression levels of Lyp1-K10XR resulted in increased temperature sensitivity even in wildtype cells (Figure 5C), demonstrating that accumulation of Lyp1 at the PM is toxic to the cell during heat stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data in Figure 5C showing reduced growth of wildtype cells expressing Lyp1-K10XR from the TDH3 promoter at elevated temperatures.

claim: Lyp1-K10XR is efficiently delivered to the plasma membrane but cannot be internalized or degraded by the heat-induced endocytic response.
source: Importantly, the Lyp1-K10XR protein is efficiently delivered to the PM but cannot be internalized or degraded by the heat-induced endocytic response (Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and Western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3 showing Lyp1-K10XR localization at the plasma membrane and protein stability during heat stress.

claim: The increased temperature sensitivity observed when Lyp1 accumulates at the plasma membrane correlates with increased PI staining during heat shock.
source: Importantly, the increased temperature sensitivity observed when Lyp1 accumulates at the PM correlates with increased PI staining during heat shock (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5D showing increased PI staining in cells with higher Lyp1 expression levels during heat stress.

claim: Increasing expression of Art1 protects against loss of PM integrity caused by Lyp1 accumulation.
source: However, protection against this loss of PM integrity could be conferred upon increasing expression of Art1 (Figure 5E), which prevents integral membrane protein accumulation at the surface (Lin et al., 2008; MacGurn et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5E showing reduced PI staining when Art1 is overexpressed in cells with high Lyp1 expression.

claim: Abrogation of either Golgi quality control (Δvps10, Δgga1, Δtul1) or ER quality control (Δdoa10, Δhrd1, Δire1) systems significantly enhances the PM integrity defect observed for Δart1 mutant cells during heat stress.
source: For example, abrogation of either Golgi quality control (Δvps10, Δgga1, Δtul1) or ER quality control (Δdoa10, Δhrd1, Δire1) systems significantly enhanced the PM integrity defect observed for Δart1 mutant cells during heat stress (Figure 6C,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6C,D showing increased PI staining in double mutants combining Δart1 with ER or Golgi quality control mutations.

claim: Cells with defects in all three integral membrane quality control systems (ERQC, GQC, and PM quality control; Δart1Δdoa10Δgga1 triple mutant cells) exhibit dramatic loss of PM integrity (∼55% of total cell population) following 3 hr at 40°C.
source: Furthermore, cells with defects in all three integral membrane quality control systems (ERQC, GQC, and PM quality control; Δart1Δdoa10Δgga1 triple mutant cells) exhibited dramatic loss of PM integrity (∼55% of total cell population) following 3 hr at 40°C (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6D showing approximately 55% PI-positive cells in Δart1Δdoa10Δgga1 triple mutants after heat stress.

claim: Mutations that abrogate either ERQC or GQC, or abrogate both ERQC and GQC, do not result in temperature sensitive growth or significant PI-positive staining of cells following heat stress.
source: Importantly, mutations that abrogate either ERQC or GQC, or abrogate both ERQC and GQC, do not result in temperature sensitive growth or significant PI-positive staining of cells following heat stress (Figure 6D), suggesting that PM quality control can compensate for defects in quality control along the secretory pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6D showing minimal PI staining in ER and Golgi quality control mutants without Δart1.

claim: PM quality control can compensate for defects in quality control along the secretory pathway.
source: Importantly, mutations that abrogate either ERQC or GQC, or abrogate both ERQC and GQC, do not result in temperature sensitive growth or significant PI-positive staining of cells following heat stress (Figure 6D), suggesting that PM quality control can compensate for defects in quality control along the secretory pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ER and Golgi quality control mutants alone do not show defects, but show synthetic defects with PM quality control mutants.

claim: The ART-Rsp5 ubiquitin ligase network comprises a plasma membrane quality control system that protects yeast cells from proteotoxic stress.
source: Here we describe a quality control function of the Rsp5-ART ubiquitin ligase adaptor network that functions to protect plasma membrane (PM) integrity.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence showing the role of Rsp5 and ART proteins in protecting cells during heat stress.

claim: Failure to mediate the protective response during heat stress leads to toxic accumulation of misfolded integral membrane proteins at the cell surface.
source: Failure to mediate this protective response during heat stress leads to toxic accumulation of misfolded integral membrane proteins at the cell surface, which causes loss of PM integrity and cell death.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing cargo accumulation, PI staining, and temperature sensitivity in mutants defective for the ART-Rsp5 system.

claim: Toxic accumulation of misfolded integral membrane proteins at the cell surface causes loss of PM integrity and cell death.
source: Failure to mediate this protective response during heat stress leads to toxic accumulation of misfolded integral membrane proteins at the cell surface, which causes loss of PM integrity and cell death.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing PI staining (loss of PM integrity) and temperature sensitivity (cell death) in mutants that accumulate cargo at the plasma membrane.

claim: The Rsp5-ART network targets the degradation of proteins that have exceeded their functional lifetime due to damage and/or misfolding.
source: Thus, the Rsp5-ART network comprises a PM quality control system that works together with sequential quality control pathways in the ER and Golgi to (i) target the degradation of proteins that have exceeded their functional lifetime due to damage and/or misfolding and (ii) limit the toxic accumulation of specific proteins at the cell surface during proteotoxic stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that the ART-Rsp5 system targets cargo for degradation during heat stress and other proteotoxic conditions.

claim: The Rsp5-ART network limits the toxic accumulation of specific proteins at the cell surface during proteotoxic stress.
source: Thus, the Rsp5-ART network comprises a PM quality control system that works together with sequential quality control pathways in the ER and Golgi to (i) target the degradation of proteins that have exceeded their functional lifetime due to damage and/or misfolding and (ii) limit the toxic accumulation of specific proteins at the cell surface during proteotoxic stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that loss of the ART-Rsp5 system leads to cargo accumulation and toxicity during heat stress.

claim: Misfolded protein domains that are soluble and accessible to the cytosol can be targeted for degradation by CHIP, an E3 ligase that interacts with various chaperones.
source: For example, misfolded protein domains that are soluble and accessible to the cytosol can be targeted for degradation by CHIP, an E3 ligase that interacts with various chaperones to target ubiquitination of misfolded substrates (Meacham et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Meacham et al., 2001.

claim: Unfolded soluble protein domains in the lumen of the ER are clients of the Hsp70 family member BiP/Kar2.
source: Similarly, unfolded soluble protein domains in the lumen of the ER are clients of the Hsp70 family member BiP/Kar2, and extended association with BiP/Kar2 can lead to targeting for ubiquitination by the ERAD machinery and subsequent proteasomal degradation (Claessen et al., 2011; Walter and Ron, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Claessen et al., 2011 and Walter and Ron, 2011.

claim: Extended association with BiP/Kar2 can lead to targeting for ubiquitination by the ERAD machinery and subsequent proteasomal degradation.
source: Similarly, unfolded soluble protein domains in the lumen of the ER are clients of the Hsp70 family member BiP/Kar2, and extended association with BiP/Kar2 can lead to targeting for ubiquitination by the ERAD machinery and subsequent proteasomal degradation (Claessen et al., 2011; Walter and Ron, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Claessen et al., 2011 and Walter and Ron, 2011.

claim: Most post-ER integral membrane proteins are degraded via lysosomal trafficking.
source: In contrast to proteins in the cytosol or the ER, which are degraded by the proteasome, most post-ER integral membrane proteins are degraded via lysosomal trafficking.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about protein degradation pathways.

claim: Lysosomal trafficking of post-ER integral membrane proteins is typically ubiquitin-dependent.
source: This process is typically ubiquitin-dependent and involves: (i) selective recognition of cargo for ubiquitination, (ii) capture of ubiquitinated cargo for trafficking to the endosome, (iii) endosomal sorting by ESCRT complexes, which package ubiquitinated cargo into vesicles that bud into the lumen of the endosome (intralumenal vesicles, or ILVs), and (iv) fusion of these multivesicular endosomes with lysosomal/vacuolar compartments, resulting in cargo degradation (Henne et al., 2011; MacGurn et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Henne et al., 2011 and MacGurn et al., 2012.

claim: A peripheral membrane protein quality control system was identified for the detection, ubiquitination, and downregulation of misfolded CFTR from the plasma membrane.
source: Recently, a peripheral membrane protein quality control system was identified for the detection, ubiquitination, and downregulation of misfolded CFTR from the plasma membrane. This mechanism involves recognition of the misfolded cytosolic domain of CFTR by molecular chaperones (Hsc70 and Hsp90) which then recruit the E3 ubiquitin ligase CHIP to ubiquitinate misfolded CFTR (Okiyoneda et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Okiyoneda et al., 2010.

claim: Recognition of misfolded CFTR involves molecular chaperones (Hsc70 and Hsp90) which recruit the E3 ubiquitin ligase CHIP.
source: This mechanism involves recognition of the misfolded cytosolic domain of CFTR by molecular chaperones (Hsc70 and Hsp90) which then recruit the E3 ubiquitin ligase CHIP to ubiquitinate misfolded CFTR (Okiyoneda et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Okiyoneda et al., 2010.

claim: A similar mechanism to CFTR quality control functions in the endocytic downregulation of artificial PM cargo fused to cytosolic domains that undergo temperature-induced misfolding.
source: Importantly, a similar mechanism was shown to function in the endocytic downregulation of artificial PM cargo fused to cytosolic domains that undergo temperature-induced misfolding (Apaja et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Apaja et al., 2010.

claim: Early studies of Pma1 report its rapid degradation following heat stress.
source: For example, early studies of Pma1, the yeast plasma membrane H+-ATPase, report its rapid degradation following heat stress (Piper, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Piper, 1995.

claim: An unstable mutant allele of Pma1 is rapidly ubiquitinated, endocytosed, and degraded in the yeast vacuole and may represent a misfolded form of the protein.
source: More recent studies have proposed that an unstable mutant allele of Pma1 which is rapidly ubiquitinated, endocytosed, and degraded in the yeast vacuole may represent a misfolded form of the protein (Liu and Chang, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liu and Chang, 2006.

claim: Loss of sphingolipids alters the activity and stability of Gap1 at the cell surface.
source: Other studies of the yeast general amino acid transporter Gap1 demonstrate that loss of sphingolipids alters the activity and stability of Gap1 at the cell surface, suggesting that proteins may become misfolded when PM lipid composition is altered (Lauwers et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lauwers et al., 2007.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae can tolerate a wide range of temperatures for growth.
source: Given its dramatic affect on surface protein stability, and given the ability of Saccharomyces cerevisiae to tolerate a wide range of temperatures for growth (Steinmetz et al., 2002), we decided to further investigate the molecular basis for heat-induced endocytic downregulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Steinmetz et al., 2002.

claim: Propidium iodide (PI) is a polar fluorescent vital dye that binds to nucleic acids but is membrane impermeant.
source: To better understand the basis of this temperature sensitive phenotype, we utilized a polar fluorescent vital dye, propidium iodide (PI, MW = 668.4 Da), which binds to nucleic acids but is membrane impermeant.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the properties of propidium iodide.

claim: PI staining can be used to score the number of cells in a population that have lost cellular integrity.
source: Thus, PI staining can be used to score the number of cells in a population that have lost cellular integrity.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the use of PI as a viability marker.

claim: Wildtype yeast cells grown at 26°C exhibit negligible (<1%) PI-positive cells within the population.
source: For example, wildtype yeast cells grown at 26°C exhibit negligible (<1%) PI-positive cells within the population (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3A showing minimal PI staining in wildtype cells at 26°C.

claim: Yeast cells heat-shocked at 65°C for 10 min or treated with nystatin show 100% PI-positive staining.
source: However, if these same yeast cells are heat-shocked (65°C for 10 min) or treated with the drug nystatin, which binds to ergosterol and forms pores in the yeast plasma membrane, all yeast cells (100%) stain positive for PI (Figure 3A), demonstrating the utility of PI as a marker for PM integrity.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3A showing complete PI staining after severe heat shock or nystatin treatment.

claim: Nystatin binds to ergosterol and forms pores in the yeast plasma membrane.
source: However, if these same yeast cells are heat-shocked (65°C for 10 min) or treated with the drug nystatin, which binds to ergosterol and forms pores in the yeast plasma membrane, all yeast cells (100%) stain positive for PI (Figure 3A), demonstrating the utility of PI as a marker for PM integrity.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the mechanism of action of nystatin.

claim: Overexpression of ART2 can suppress the temperature sensitive phenotype of Δart1 mutant cells.
source: All multicopy overexpression plasmids that suppressed the Δart1 temperature sensitive growth defect (84 total suppressors isolated) were found to encode either ART1 (35 individual isolates) or ART2 (49 individual isolates) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic suppressor screen data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Multiple ART family proteins may protect cells during heat stress.
source: The identification of ART2 as a suppressor of the Δart1 temperature sensitivity phenotype indicated that (i) multiple ART family proteins may protect cells during heat stress and (ii) different ART proteins may have overlapping cargo specificities which create redundancy in the system.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ART2 overexpression can suppress Δart1 temperature sensitivity.

claim: Different ART proteins may have overlapping cargo specificities which create redundancy in the system.
source: The identification of ART2 as a suppressor of the Δart1 temperature sensitivity phenotype indicated that (i) multiple ART family proteins may protect cells during heat stress and (ii) different ART proteins may have overlapping cargo specificities which create redundancy in the system.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ART2 can functionally substitute for ART1 when overexpressed.

claim: The ART modular adaptor network mediates the recognition and ubiquitination of cell surface proteins, thereby directing the endocytic remodeling of PM protein composition.
source: Previously, we identified and characterized a network of Rsp5 ubiquitin ligase adaptors called ARTS, or arrestin-related trafficking adaptors. The ART modular adaptor network mediates the recognition and ubiquitination of cell surface proteins, thereby directing the endocytic remodeling of PM protein composition.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work by the authors establishing the function of the ART network.

claim: ART proteins serve as a key point of regulation during changes in nutrient availability and environmental stress.
source: Thus, ART proteins serve as a key point of regulation during changes in nutrient availability and environmental stress.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work and the current findings showing ART function during stress.

claim: The ART-Rsp5 quality surveillance mechanism at the PM functions in parallel with both ER and Golgi QC systems.
source: The ART-Rsp5 quality surveillance mechanism at the PM functions in parallel with both ER and Golgi QC systems to control both the quality and quantity of integral membrane proteins in the cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction data showing synthetic defects when PM, ER, and Golgi quality control systems are disrupted together.

claim: Mutations in quality control systems that affect soluble cytosolic proteins do not interact genetically with mutations that affect quality control of integral membrane proteins.
source: In general, mutations that affected quality control of soluble cytosolic proteins did not interact genetically with mutations that affected quality control of integral membrane proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by the genetic interaction data in Figure 6B showing no synthetic defects between cytosolic QC and membrane QC mutations.

claim: The complete network of ART adaptors is predicted to contain 173 disordered regions.
source: Indeed, while San1 is predicted to contain 12 disordered regions, the complete network of ART adaptors is predicted to contain 173 disordered regions (some greater than 100 amino acids in length) demonstrating the potential capacity for this system to directly detect misfolded proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on computational prediction of disordered regions in ART proteins.

claim: San1 is predicted to contain 12 disordered regions.
source: Indeed, while San1 is predicted to contain 12 disordered regions, the complete network of ART adaptors is predicted to contain 173 disordered regions (some greater than 100 amino acids in length) demonstrating the potential capacity for this system to directly detect misfolded proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on computational prediction of disordered regions in San1.

claim: The nuclear E3 ubiquitin ligase San1 is capable of targeting the degradation of a broad range of soluble nuclear proteins by a mechanism that requires intrinsically disordered segments of the San1 protein.
source: For example, the nuclear E3 ubquitin ligase San1 is capable of targeting the degradation of a broad range of soluble nuclear proteins by a mechanism that requires intrinsically disordered segments of the San1 protein (Rosenbaum et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rosenbaum et al., 2011.

claim: The E3 ubiquitin ligase CHIP binds to Hsp70, which effectively targets chronically misfolded proteins for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation.
source: For example, the E3 ubiquitin ligase CHIP binds to Hsp70, which effectively targets chronically misfolded proteins for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation (Meacham et al., 2001; Okiyoneda et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Meacham et al., 2001 and Okiyoneda et al., 2010.

claim: The yeast genome does not encode a homolog of mammalian CHIP.
source: While the yeast genome does not encode a homolog of mammalian CHIP, the analogous proteins, Ubr1 and Ubr2, are also required for the degradation of misfolded proteins (Khosrow-Khavar et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about yeast genome content and citation to Khosrow-Khavar et al., 2012.

claim: Ubr1 and Ubr2 are required for the degradation of misfolded proteins in yeast.
source: While the yeast genome does not encode a homolog of mammalian CHIP, the analogous proteins, Ubr1 and Ubr2, are also required for the degradation of misfolded proteins (Khosrow-Khavar et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Khosrow-Khavar et al., 2012.

claim: Ubr1 and Ubr2 are dispensable for the heat-induced endocytic response associated with the turnover of integral PM proteins.
source: However, Ubr1 and Ubr2 are dispensable for the heat-induced endocytic response associated with the turnover of integral PM proteins (Figure 6B and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 6B showing no defects in Ubr1 and Ubr2 mutants during heat stress.

claim: The ARRDC family of proteins in mammalian cells encode proteins similar to ARTs with an N-terminal arrestin-domain and a C-terminal domain containing multiple PY motifs capable of binding to members of the Nedd4 family of ubiquitin ligases.
source: It is tempting to speculate that a similar peripheral quality control function may be mediated by the ARRDC family of proteins in mammalian cells, which encode proteins similar to ARTs with an N-terminal arrestin-domain and a C-terminal domain containing multiple PY motifs capable of binding to members of the Nedd4 family of ubiquitin ligases (Patwari and Lee, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Patwari and Lee, 2012.

claim: Quality control of integral plasma membrane proteins plays a critical role in many human diseases.
source: Quality control of integral plasma membrane proteins plays a critical role in many human diseases because it affects the quantity of functional proteins—ion channels, nutrient transporters, and signaling receptors—at the cell surface.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the importance of PM protein quality control in disease.

claim: Many channelopathies are likely caused by mutations that affect both the quality and quantity of specific ion channels at the cell surface.
source: Indeed, many human channelopathies, which include many neurological or cardiac disorders, are very likely caused by mutations that affect both the quality and quantity of specific ion channels at the cell surface (Kullmann, 2010; Rougier et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kullmann, 2010 and Rougier et al., 2010.
